title: Green ants

names.gloss: the big green ant that is eaten, comes in December–January
green ant, used as a medicine for the common cold

identification.basis: The dictionary has three green-ant words with their uses; Roth (1901) describes the Bloomfield method of taking and eating them in detail; the green tree ant Oecophylla smaragdina is recorded ten times within 60 km of Karma Waters.

summary: The green ant is three things in the dictionary: **[munjurr](word:munjurr)**, the ant; **[nyirran](word:nyirran)**, 'the big green ant that is eaten, comes in December–January'; and **[yangka](word:yangka)**, the medicine, 'used as a medicine for the common cold and other chest complaints. They can be crushed and the odour inhaled to cure headache; or the eggs, larvae, and pupae from the nests can be mixed with salt water and taken' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth watched the same thing done: 'green ants, as well as their larvae, are eaten as food both by men and women, and at Princess Charlotte Bay, Cooktown, Bloomfield, etc., are in addition used as medicine (e.g., in diarrhoea, headache, etc.)'; on the Bloomfield 'the nests are pulled down and their contents shaken into a piece of bark or large leaf', kneaded, squeezed into a trough of water 'which makes the water look as if milk had been added to it', and the liquid 'sopped up by means of chewed grass, while the remains of the ants and eggs are eaten' [ref:roth1901]. The ant itself, *Oecophylla smaragdina*, is the weaver ant of the tropics, which builds its nests by pulling leaves together in living chains and gluing them with the silk of its own larvae, farms scale insects for honeydew, and bites [ref:wiki-oecophylla].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[munjurr](word:munjurr)** 'green ant'. **[nyirran](word:nyirran)** 'the big green ant that is eaten, comes in December–January'. **[yangka](word:yangka)** 'green ant. These are used as a medicine for the common cold and other chest complaints. They can be crushed and the odour inhaled to cure headache; or the eggs, larvae, and pupae from the nests can be mixed with salt water and taken'. **[kurrmaja](word:kurrmaja)** 'larvae of green ants'. **[kalbal](word:kalbal)** 'the mixture made from green ant larvae/pupae and eggs eaten for chest sickness and the common cold' [ref:hershberger1982]. The other ants: **[karrkil](word:karrkil)** 'red jumper ant. Some people have gotten sick and vomited after being bitten by them'; **[ngalmnbu](word:ngalmnbu)** 'jumper ant'; **[kira-kira](word:kira-kira)** 'black ant'; **[jabarrangkul](word:jabarrangkul)** 'black ant. Also their nest in rotten logs'; **[kawa](word:kawa)** 'little ants, white or black'; **[muyu-muyu](word:muyu-muyu)** 'small red ant'; **[jingka-jingka](word:jingka-jingka)** 'honey ant, the abdomen enlarges after eating'; **[jungu-jungu](word:jungu-jungu)** 'white ant eggs'; **[jawurraji](word:jawurraji)** 'large ant bed'; **[kabay](word:kabay)** 'small ant bed' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's Bloomfield name for the moth chrysalis found in the nests was *bi-i bi-i*, and the Cooktown name *ged-ya* [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: The ant and the nest
sections.body:
'*Oecophylla smaragdina* (common names include Asian weaver ant, weaver ant, green ant, green tree ant, and orange gaster) is a species of arboreal ant found in tropical Asia and Australia. These ants form colonies with multiple nests in trees, each nest being made of leaves stitched together using' the silk of their larvae. 'Workers and major workers are mostly coloured orange. Workers are 5–7 mm long; they look after larvae and farm scale bugs for honeydew. Major workers are 8–10 mm long, with long, strong legs and large mandibles. They forage, assemble, and expand the nest. Queens are typically 20–25 mm long, and normally greenish-brown', which gives the species its name [ref:wiki-oecophylla].

'Weaver ants when constructing their leaf nests show multiphase team coordination. Workers initially spread across tree branches and pull independently on leaf edges. When one ant successfully bends a leaf segment, nearby workers stop and join to pull in unison. For leaves too wide for a single ant's span or when linking separate leaves, workers form bridges, with ants climbing onto the backs of their chain mates and pulling backward to create mechanical leverage to bring the leaf edges together.' 'The ants also attend aphids, scale insects and other homopterans to feed on the honeydew they produce, especially in tree canopies linked by lianas. For this purpose, they drive away other ant species'. 'Weaver ants can bite humans when disturbed' [ref:wiki-oecophylla].

Elsewhere in their range the same ants are food and medicine: 'the larvae and pupae are collected and processed into bird food and fish bait in Indonesia, are used in Chinese and Indian traditional medicine, and consumed as a delicacy in Thailand', where their taste is 'variously described as creamy, sour, and lemony'; 'in some parts of India, the adult ants are used in traditional medicine as a remedy for rheumatism' [ref:wiki-oecophylla].

**Roth's account, 1901.** 'Green ants, as well as their larvae, are eaten as food both by men and women, and at Princess Charlotte Bay, Cooktown, Bloomfield, etc., are in addition used as medicine (e.g., in diarrhoea, headache, etc.). At Princess Charlotte Bay and Cooktown, I have seen the nest cut down and opened on a piece of stone or rock whence the green ants scatter about in all directions, leaving the white larvae behind. Any remaining ants are removed by putting the fingers into it, letting them crawl up the arm, and rubbing them briskly off. The white larvae are then collected into more or less of a ball, rubbed a bit between the flats of the hand, and swallowed. If in large quantity, and a "big feed" wanted, the larvae from two or three nests are collected into one big ball, crumpled over with leaves, washed in water, and then eaten. The "washed" water may be also drunk. At Cape Bedford, ashes are put into the water when the ants are kneaded. On the Bloomfield (E. Hislop), the nests are pulled down and their contents shaken into a piece of bark or large leaf, and are slightly kneaded so as to prevent the grown ants getting away. The mass of squashed ants and eggs is then squeezed into a trough containing water, which makes the water look as if milk had been added to it. This liquid is sopped up by means of chewed grass, while the remains of the ants and eggs are eaten. Saltwater is preferred to fresh to mix the ants up in, and the nests are considered more palatable when there is a preponderance of eggs over ants. The "queens" are eaten without being squashed. It is interesting to note that on the Bloomfield, as well as at Cooktown, etc., the chrysalis of a lepidopteron is found in the green-ant nests. The Bloomfield blacks, who call it bi-i bi-i, consider it a great delicacy, while the Cooktown natives, who speak of it as ged-ya, break it up in water, drink the mixture, and say it is very good for bad constipation. The lower Tully River natives utilise the green ants mainly as food, but also as medicine. The insects, the young larvae at least, are either squashed up in water and drunk or else rolled up, in the dry, in "wild-ginger" leaves and baked' [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Green ant, jumper ant, meat ant
sections.body:
- **Green ant**: orange-green, long-legged, in the trees, in leaf nests, in chains; a sharp bite and a squirt of acid that stings in the bite; eaten [ref:wiki-oecophylla].
- **Jumper ants** (*karrkil*, *ngalmnbu*): big, red or black, jumping, on the ground, with a sting that has made people 'sick and vomited'; not eaten [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Meat ants and the ant beds** (*jawurraji*, *kabay*): the mound-builders of the woodland, the [echidna's](entry:echidna) food and the ant-bed of the [earth oven](entry:earth-oven) [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901].
- **Honey ant** (*jingka-jingka*): 'the abdomen enlarges after eating' [ref:hershberger1982].
- **White ants** (termites): not ants; their eggs are *jungu-jungu* and their mounds the oven stones [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Leaf nests** the size of a fist to a football, green leaves pulled together and stitched with white silk, several in one tree, on the river gums, the figs and the paperbarks [ref:wiki-oecophylla].
- **Ant highways** along the branches and the lianas, and ants on the scale insects [ref:wiki-oecophylla].
- **A nest heavy with white**: eggs and larvae, the eating stage; 'the nests are considered more palatable when there is a preponderance of eggs over ants' [ref:roth1901].
- **December and January**: the big eating ant's season [ref:hershberger1982].
- **A smell of sour lemon** on the fingers after handling the nest: the formic acid [ref:wiki-oecophylla].

sections.heading: Where they are
sections.body: In the trees along the river and the moister woodland, 'especially in tree canopies linked by lianas', from the coast to the upper Mitchell [ref:wiki-oecophylla]. The [waterhole](entry:waterhole) page's river trees are where to look; the place sections above say what is on the record locally.

sections.heading: The ant in the tree
sections.body: The green ants run the canopy they live in: they drive other ants out, farm the scale insects for honeydew, kill the caterpillars and the small things that eat leaves, and are hunted in turn by the jumping spiders that mimic their smell and by the birds [ref:wiki-oecophylla]. A moth lays its eggs in their nests, and its chrysalis was the Bloomfield delicacy *bi-i bi-i* [ref:roth1901]. The [echidna](entry:echidna) cannot reach them; the [witchetty grub](entry:witchetty-grub) page has the other insects that were eaten, and the [native bees](entry:native-bees) the other sweet thing in the trees.

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: 'The big green ant that is eaten, comes in December–January', the build-up and the first storms, when the nests are full of eggs and larvae [ref:hershberger1982]. The medicine was taken whenever a cold or a headache came, and the nests are there all year [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Food**: the larvae, pupae and eggs rolled into a ball and swallowed; the whole nest squeezed into water and the milky water sopped up with chewed grass (*wuju*); the larvae baked in wild-ginger leaves on the Tully; the queens eaten whole [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Medicine for colds and chest complaints**: *kalbal*, the eggs, larvae and pupae mixed with salt water and drunk; for headache, the ants crushed and the smell inhaled; for diarrhoea, in Roth's note [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901].
- **The moth chrysalis** from the nests: a delicacy at Bloomfield, a cure for constipation at Cooktown [ref:roth1901].
- **Bait and bird food** elsewhere in their range [ref:wiki-oecophylla].

sections.heading: Taking a green-ant nest
sections.body:
From Roth's Bloomfield and Cooktown accounts and the dictionary [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982]:

1. **Choose a nest heavy with white**, eggs and larvae rather than ants, in the eating season [ref:roth1901].
2. **Cut or pull the nest down** quickly into a sheet of bark or a big leaf; the ants bite and spray, so be quick and brush them off up the arm 'briskly' [ref:roth1901] [ref:wiki-oecophylla].
3. **For a snack**: open the nest on a rock, let the ants scatter, collect the white larvae into a ball, rub it between the palms, and swallow it [ref:roth1901].
4. **For a feed**: larvae from two or three nests into one ball, wrapped in leaves and washed in water; drink the water too [ref:roth1901].
5. **The Bloomfield way**: knead the whole contents lightly so the ants cannot escape, squeeze the mass into a trough of water, salt water for choice, until it is milky; sop it up with a grass sponge (*wuju*) and eat what is left [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982].
6. **For a cold**: eggs, larvae and pupae in salt water, drunk, *kalbal*; for a headache, crush ants and breathe the smell [ref:hershberger1982].
7. **Baked**: roll the larvae in [wild-ginger](entry:wild-ginger) leaves and bake them in the ashes, the Tully method [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Green ants bite and spray formic acid; a nest dropped on the head is a bad minute. Eyes shut, work fast [ref:wiki-oecophylla].
- The red jumper ant *karrkil* is the one that has made people 'sick and vomited'; it is not the green ant and is not eaten [ref:hershberger1982].
- Anyone who reacts to insect stings should treat ant medicine with care.
- Take a nest or two from a tree, not all of them; the colony is many nests [ref:wiki-oecophylla].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The method is as Roth saw it and the dictionary records it: a nest, a sheet of bark, a trough of water, a grass sponge; the medicine for a cold is the same recipe [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982]. It is the easiest of the old foods to try and one of the sharpest-tasting.

locations.summary: Green ants live in the Hann country: the Atlas of Living Australia holds 14 records of *Oecophylla smaragdina* from 1980 to 2022 around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:ala-hann-ants]. Roth saw green-ant nests eaten at Princess Charlotte Bay, and a Kuku Warra man from the Laura side told the Federal Court in 2023 how the nest is crushed in water for a headache [ref:roth1901] [ref:fca-kukuwarra].

sections.heading: Where they are here
sections.body: The Atlas of Living Australia holds 14 green-ant records from a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru, from 1980 to 2022 [ref:ala-hann-ants]. That is a thin record for a common ant, so treat it as 'they live here', not as a map. Look for the leaf nests in the trees along the river, 'especially in tree canopies linked by lianas' [ref:wiki-oecophylla].

sections.heading: How the people of this country used them
sections.body:
**Princess Charlotte Bay, c. 1900.** Roth: green ants 'at Princess Charlotte Bay, Cooktown, Bloomfield, etc., are in addition used as medicine (e.g., in diarrhoea, headache, etc.). At Princess Charlotte Bay and Cooktown, I have seen the nest cut down and opened on a piece of stone or rock whence the green ants scatter about in all directions, leaving the white larvae behind.' The larvae were rolled into a ball between the hands and swallowed [ref:roth1901].

**Kuku Warra (Laura and the Palmer side), 2023.** 'With green ants, you crush the nest, mix it with water and it cures a headache too. If you catch the ants at the right time of the year they have white eggs, and when you crush the eggs with water, it makes a milky drink' [ref:fca-kukuwarra]. He does not say which time of year; on the coast the dictionary gives December–January for the big eating ant [ref:hershberger1982]. See [bush medicine](entry:bush-medicine).

Nothing about green ants is published from the Thaypan or Possum evidence for the Hann itself.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country; Laura and the Deighton River side are Kuku Warra country; all three were determined on 2 November 2023 [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan] [ref:fca-kukuwarra]. Taking a nest for food or medicine is part of native title for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal needs [ref:nta1993].

locations.summary: Green ants are in the river trees at [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters): the Atlas holds ten records within 60 km of the homestead [ref:ala-karma-60].

sections.heading: Where they are here
sections.body: Ten records within 60 km of the Karma Waters homestead, in the river trees [ref:ala-karma-60]. The method in the general section works here as anywhere: a nest, a sheet of bark, a trough of water, a grass sponge [ref:roth1901].

locations.summary: On the Bloomfield green ants were food and medicine both. Roth's Bloomfield informant described the milky drink of squeezed nests, and the moth chrysalis in the nests, *bi-i bi-i*, was 'a great delicacy' [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Gathered here in the 1970s
sections.body: Anderson lists 'insects such as green ants and their eggs' among the gathered foods at Bloomfield in the 1970s [ref:anderson1996].
